messages.floating: Nothing is pulling on it, so it just floats.
messages.boundary: It drifted until it reached the wall.
messages.timeout: Still falling when the timer ran out.
messages.landed: Landed after {{time}} seconds, hitting the ground at {{speed}} m/s.
messages.landedTerminal: Landed after {{time}} seconds at {{speed}} m/s — as fast as the air will let it fall.

drop.credits: Motion is integrated with RK4 at a fixed 1/240 s step. With air off, the closed-form constant-acceleration solution is used instead — which is why every object lands together in a vacuum, whatever its mass.

blurbs.beginner: Gravity pulls the object down, so it speeds up the whole way. With air resistance on, the air pushes back harder the faster it falls.
blurbs.intermediate: Gravity gives a constant downward acceleration. Drag opposes the velocity and grows with its square, so the acceleration shrinks until the two balance at terminal velocity.

kindBlurbs.bouncy: They bounce apart and keep all their energy. Nothing is lost.
kindBlurbs.sticky: They join together on impact and move off as one lump.
kindBlurbs.realistic: What usually happens: they bounce, but lose some energy as heat and sound.

messages.neverMeet: These two will never meet — give them speeds that bring them together.
messages.stuck: They stuck together and moved off {{direction}} at {{speed}} m/s. {{percent}}% of the energy was lost as heat and sound — but the total momentum did not change.
messages.bouncedIntro: {{nameA}} went off {{directionA}} at {{speedA}} m/s, {{nameB}} {{directionB}} at {{speedB}} m/s.
messages.bouncedLossless: {{intro}} They kept all of their energy, and the total momentum is exactly what it was before.
messages.bouncedLossy: {{intro}} They lost {{percent}}% of their energy as heat and sound, but the total momentum is unchanged.

collisions.credits: Momentum (mass × speed, added up) is the same before and after every collision here — that is a law, not an approximation. Energy is only preserved when the objects are perfectly bouncy.

blurbs.beginner: When the two objects meet they push on each other and swap some of their motion. How bouncy they are decides whether they spring apart or stay stuck together.
blurbs.intermediate: Total momentum before the impact equals total momentum after it, whatever the collision type. The coefficient of restitution sets how much kinetic energy survives.

circuits.wiringHint: Series: the same current passes through both bulbs. Parallel: both bulbs get the full battery voltage and draw their own current.

toggles.switchOn: The loop is complete — current can flow
toggles.switchOff: The loop is broken — nothing lights up

messages.switchOpen: The switch is open, so no current can flow.
messages.noCurrent: The loop is complete, but no current is flowing.
messages.dim: Current is flowing — the bulb glows faintly.
messages.glowing: Current is flowing at a comfortable brightness.
messages.bright: Current is flowing hard — the bulb is glowing brightly.
messages.oneBurnedOut: {{name}} burned out from too much power and has gone dark.
messages.bothBurnedOut: Both bulbs burned out from too much power and have gone dark.

circuits.credits: Every reading is computed directly from Ohm's Law for the wiring you have chosen — nothing here is a scripted animation.

blurbs.beginner: Electricity needs a complete loop to flow. Close the switch and it runs from the battery, through the bulb, and back — more electricity through the bulb means a brighter glow.
blurbs.intermediate: Voltage drives current around the loop, and resistance opposes it. In series the same current passes through every bulb; in parallel each bulb gets the full battery voltage and draws its own current.

intro.title: What is a magnet?
intro.body: Every magnet has two ends called poles — one North, one South. Bring a North pole next to a South pole and they pull together. Bring two matching poles together (North-North or South-South) and they push apart.
intro.tip: Try switching to Repel below and watch the arrows flip!

sliders.strengthHint: How powerful this magnet is — a bigger number means a stronger pull or push.

magnets.orientationHint: Attract: opposite poles face each other. Repel: matching poles face each other.

messages.pullingWeak: The magnets are pulling together, gently.
messages.pullingStrong: The magnets are pulling together hard.
messages.pushingWeak: The magnets are pushing apart, gently.
messages.pushingStrong: The magnets are pushing apart hard.
messages.snapped: The magnets pulled in and snapped together!

magnets.formulaNote: This uses a simplified pole-strength model (like Coulomb's law), not the full magnetic dipole field equations.
magnets.credits: Force is computed live from F = k·p₁·p₂ / r² for whatever poles and distance you set — nothing here is a scripted animation.

blurbs.beginner: Every magnet has two ends called poles: North and South. Facing opposite poles (North to South) pulls the magnets together. Facing matching poles (North to North, or South to South) pushes them apart.
blurbs.intermediate: The force between two magnetic poles falls off with the square of the distance between them, just like gravity and electric charge. Facing opposite poles pulls the magnets together; facing matching poles pushes them apart.

outcomes.timeout: Still falling at the time limit
outcomes.floating: No net force — it just floats

notes.rose: It rose {{height}} m above where it started before falling back down.
notes.terminal: It stopped speeding up on the way down: air resistance grew until it exactly balanced the object's weight.
notes.timeout: It was still falling when the timer ran out. Try a smaller drop height, or turn air resistance off.
